units.evidence_span: Non-RTP customers, like residential and small commercial customers, are subject to separate rates to collect base revenues and fuel revenues.

units.evidence_span: This will assist in reducing FCR rates for FCR customers, but may increase base rates for those same customers

units.sentence: If the PSC adopts any proposed plan, your fuel charge would likely rise, but base rates could later drop to return the same money.
units.evidence_span: This will assist in reducing FCR rates for FCR customers, but may increase base rates for those same customers
units.problem: Both directions are reversed, and the cited passages say the opposite (span above is from P-105). Every proposed plan raises the fuel credit (P-058, P-115), and a bigger credit lowers the fuel charge for standard-rate customers such as homes (P-144: FCR customers 'pay all fuel costs net of the RTP Fuel Credit'). The matching base-side loss pushes base rates up, not down (P-115: 'increasing the RTP fuel credit would put upward pressure on base rates'). It also contradicts the page's own lines 9, 15 and 143-144.
units.suggested_fix: If the PSC adopts any proposed plan, your fuel charge would likely drop, but base rates could later rise to recover the same money.

units.sentence: Whether you come out ahead depends on the next base rate case.
units.evidence_span: The direction and magnitude of any future impact would need to be determined in a base rate case.

units.sentence: No filing we read gives a typical home's net.
units.marker: {editorial: scoped to the filings we read; Georgia Power's per-$100 million figures (P-142, P-143) are examples, not a plan's effect}
units.reason: Consistent with the passages: Staff's $1.35 (P-066) is a fuel-only look-back, and P-141 to P-143 are per-$100 million examples. Line 36 contradicts this tag.

units.sentence: If you run a business on Georgia Power's standard rates: Your fuel charge will drop, but base rates could later rise to recover the same money.
units.evidence_span: This will assist in reducing FCR rates for FCR customers, but may increase base rates for those same customers
units.problem: The direction is right, but the condition is dropped and the outcome is stated as certain. Nothing has been adopted: the order says the PSC 'may make modifications if appropriate' (P-016). 'Will drop' turns a possible result into a fact, and it doesn't match the home line's 'If the PSC adopts any proposed plan ... would likely'.
units.suggested_fix: If the PSC adopts any proposed plan, your fuel charge would likely drop, but base rates could later rise to recover the same money.

units.sentence: No party whose testimony we could read backs today's method in every part, so Plan A's line is GAM's argument against a bigger credit.
units.marker: {editorial: scoped; GAM accepts either take-or-pay option if the PSC finds a change is needed (P-111)}
units.reason: Consistent with the passages: Georgia Power, PIA Staff and GIPL all propose changes (P-055, P-058, P-073, P-095), and GAM accepts either option if a change is needed (P-111). Minor: 'argument against a bigger credit' is better put as GAM's warning about base rates (P-115).

units.sentence: Resource Supply Management's testimony, a scan we could not read, isn't covered.
units.reason: Process note.

framing_issues.text: Plan C is the best choice for most homes
framing_issues.issue: The page recommends an option. That breaks the rule of no ratings or endorsements, and no filing supports it: the page itself says no plan's net home effect is known. It sits in the values guide, which should give only parties' own words.

framing_issues.text: your fuel charge would likely rise, but base rates could later drop
framing_issues.issue: Gets the main trade-off backwards for the biggest audience (homes). It contradicts line 9, line 15, lines 143-144 and every party's account, so a home reader would think the plans raise their fuel bill.

framing_issues.text: are what PIA Staff's plan would do for a typical home
framing_issues.issue: Presents a per-$100 million example as one plan's effect. That makes Plan C look measured for homes when no plan is, and together with line 166 it tilts the page toward Plan C. It also contradicts the sentence before it and line 144.

framing_issues.text: it also sets your power company's rates
framing_issues.issue: Gets wrong which customers the case covers: it tells EMC and city-owned utility customers that this Georgia Power case sets their rates. The next sentence, quoting the PSC FAQ (P-170), contradicts it.

framing_issues.text: PIA Staff's witness panel, which backs Plan B
framing_issues.issue: The values guide names the wrong party for the plan. It credits PIA Staff with Georgia Power's pipeline proposal, which PIA Staff calls 'only a partial solution' (P-082), so readers can't map their value to the right party.
States an outcome that hasn't been decided as certain. It drops 'if the PSC adopts...' and 'likely', so it doesn't match the home line and overstates what the record shows.
The main 'how to reach them' line has a different local number from lines 45 and 47 (404-656-4501). A reader can't tell which is right, and the one here is wrong per P-163.

framing_issues.text: second and fourth Tuesday of each month
framing_issues.issue: Wrong meeting days. They also conflict with the page's own Dec 15, 2026 decision date, which is a third Tuesday.
Conflicts with the Plan C section (lines 188-189: about $126 million). It overstates Staff's 2026 estimate by about 29 percent in the summary readers see first.

framing_issues.text: GAM, a manufacturers' group, argues against a bigger credit (also lines 162 and 166)
framing_issues.issue: Overstates GAM's position. GAM warns of upward pressure on base rates (P-115) and opposes crediting real-time money against pipeline fees (P-110), but says either take-or-pay option 'would adequately address' the concerns if a change is needed (P-111).
Stated in the page's own voice. It is Georgia Power's statement (P-054), and lines 30 and 118 attribute it that way.
The heading reads like the time of the decision. P-024 gives only the session's start, and line 48 says the time this case comes up isn't posted.
